22.title: The boy at the door
22.hook: Parvati shapes a son from earth and breathes life into him; why families welcome Ganesha into clay
22.carry: the holy can live in clay
22.tomorrow: the boy says no to the next one at the door. who is it?
22.howItsDone: At Ganesh Chaturthi many families bring home a clay Ganesha, invite him in with prana pratishtha, and after a day and a half to ten days immerse the image in water (visarjan). His birth story is often retold then.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the first camp on a battlefield, with Krishna's line: you have the right to act, not to the fruit. Now the stories start, and the first one starts at a closed door.
screen: `YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO ACT. NOT TO THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Parvati lives with Shiva on Mount Kailash, and every guard at the door is one of his ganas, his attendants, loyal to him. Whenever Shiva wants in, they step aside. Nobody in that house is simply hers. So before her bath she takes the paste she rubbed on her skin, the earth of her own body, and shapes a boy. Then she breathes life into him. The first face he ever sees is his mother's. She hands him a staff and gives him one job: guard this door. No one comes in.
screen: `NOBODY IN THE HOUSE IS HERS.` → `A BOY SHAPED FROM EARTH.` → `SHE BREATHES LIFE INTO HIM.` → `NO ONE COMES IN.`

segments.voice: That boy grows up to be Ganesha, the god you met on day one. This telling is the Shiva Purana's, a collection of stories about Shiva, and it isn't the only version. Notice what he's made of. Not thunder, not light. Earth, shaped by the Goddess's hands, with her breath in it. Hindu homes still act this story out. Every year at Ganesh Chaturthi, many families bring home a Ganesha shaped from clay. With prayers they invite him to live in it, a rite called prana pratishtha: setting the breath in. For a few days he's the guest of honor, fed, sung to, visited by the whole street. Then they carry him to a river or the sea, and give the clay back to the water. The teaching under it: God can be welcomed into something as ordinary as earth, and loved there, without being trapped there. That's one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: God isn't only far off in the sky. God can be found in what's right in front of you, even a handful of earth. And somewhere down the mountain, someone very large is walking home.

segments.voice: For two minutes, pick up something ordinary near you that matters to you: a ring, a mug, a photo. Hold it. Notice that it's just stuff, and also not. Something you love has been breathed into it. Then set it down gently. It's still yours.
Ganas: Shiva's attendants, the guards of his house. Keep an eye on them. The boy made of earth is going to end up leading them.

segments.voice: Your line: the holy can live in clay. Parvati shaped hers from earth. See you tomorrow.

23.title: Parvati's grief
23.hook: Shiva meets the boy at his own door; Parvati's grief, the Goddess's power, stops the universe
23.tomorrow: Shiva has to bring the boy back. so where does he find a head?
23.howItsDone: Many Hindus worship God as the Mother, Shakti, in forms like Parvati, Durga and Kali, and call on her simply as Ma. This story is told as part of Ganesha's birth, often at Ganesh Chaturthi.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a boy made of earth, set at his mother's door with one job. The holy can live in clay. Today someone walks up to that door.
screen: `THE HOLY CAN LIVE IN CLAY.`

segments.voice: Here's a comment you might see under a video of a Ganesha festival: wait, his own dad cut his head off? Fair question, and the story has an answer. Why would a story like that be told at a festival full of kids? Start where it starts. Shiva walks home up the mountain to his own house, and at his own door is a boy he has never seen. You can't come in, says the boy. This is my house, says Shiva. My mother said no one. Shiva sends his ganas. The boy beats them back. In the Shiva Purana, even the gods can't get past him. Then Shiva raises his trident.
screen: `WAIT, HIS OWN DAD?` → `A STRANGER AT HIS OWN DOOR.` → `THE BOY SAYS NO.` → `THE TRIDENT.`

segments.voice: So, the puzzle. The story doesn't make anyone the villain. The boy is keeping his word to his mother. Shiva is trying to walk into his own home. Both are right, and something terrible happens anyway. Then Parvati comes out. In the Shiva Purana her grief is so big that she calls up fierce goddesses, forms of her own power, and sends them to swallow the universe. Narada and the gods come pleading, and she names her terms: bring my son back, and honor him among you. And Shiva, the great god, does what she asks. Here's the teaching. In Hinduism, God isn't only Father. God is also Mother, and her name is Shakti: power, the energy that moves everything. Parvati is one face of her; Durga and Kali, with their weapons, are others. Many Hindus pray to her simply as Ma. A saying many know plays on the letters: take the i of Shakti out of Shiva, and you get shava, a corpse. The god and his power can't be pulled apart. Nobody tells this mother to calm down. Her grief is the power of the universe, and even Shiva answers it. That's why a story like this can be told at a festival full of kids: it's a mother's love, bringing her child home.
screen: `BOTH OF THEM ARE RIGHT.` · `HER GRIEF STOPS THE UNIVERSE.` · `SHAKTI: GOD AS MOTHER, GOD AS POWER.` · `SHIVA WITHOUT SHAKTI: SHAVA.` · then, large: `GOD IS ALSO MOTHER: SHAKTI.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, bring to mind the strongest woman you know, the one whose care held your world together: a mother, a grandmother, an aunt, a teacher. Many Hindus pray to the Goddess with one word, Ma, said softly on the out-breath; if you pray, try it. If you don't, say her name instead, with a quiet thank you.
Trident: Shiva's three-pointed spear, trishula in Sanskrit, three spears. Raised at a door, it set off a grief even Shiva had to answer.
screen: `TRIDENT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Hold onto this one: God is also Mother, and her name is Shakti. Even Shiva answers her. Day twenty-three, done.

24.title: The elephant head
24.hook: Shiva brings the boy back with an elephant's head and promises he'll be worshipped first
24.tomorrow: two brothers race around the world. how does the slow one win?
24.howItsDone: Many Hindus begin weddings, housewarmings, new ventures and other ceremonies by honoring Ganesha first, often with a short prayer or mantra to him before anything else begins.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the trident, and a mother's grief that stopped the universe until even Shiva answered. God is also Mother, Shakti. Now Shiva has to keep his word.
screen: `GOD IS ALSO MOTHER: SHAKTI.`

segments.voice: Every family has a story two relatives tell differently, each sure the other got it wrong. Ganesha's head is one of those, and here the relatives are old texts. Here's the Shiva Purana's telling. Go north, Shiva tells his ganas. Bring back the head of the first living creature you meet. They run down the mountain into the forests, and the first creature they find is an elephant. Shiva sets its head on the boy's body and breathes life into him. The boy opens his eyes for the second time in his life, and his mother is there again. Now he has a trunk, wide ears, and the face you already know.
screen: `TWO RELATIVES, TWO VERSIONS.` → `GO NORTH.` → `AN ELEPHANT.` → `HE OPENS HIS EYES AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Now the debate, and it's a real one among people who love him. Why an elephant? One side says: the text's answer is plain. It was the first creature they met. The head is chance, and the point of the story is what Shiva does next. The other side says: look at that face. Big ears, to listen more than he speaks. A trunk that can uproot a tree or pick up one grain of rice. An elephant doesn't go around the forest; it walks through and makes a path. That fits a remover of obstacles too well to shrug off. And the texts don't even agree on how the head was lost: in the Brahmavaivarta Purana, it happens when Shani, the god of the planet Saturn, looks at the baby. The tradition keeps both tellings side by side. What they share is the ending. Shiva makes the boy leader of the ganas, the very guards who fought him: Ganesha, Ganapati, lord of the ganas. And he promises the boy will be worshipped first, before any god, before any ceremony. That promise is why Hindus begin with Ganesha: a wedding, a housewarming, a new business, even a child's first day of school often starts with a prayer to him. The newest god goes first.
screen: `WHY AN ELEPHANT?` · `ONE SIDE: THE FIRST CREATURE MET.` · `THE OTHER: THAT FACE FITS.` · `WORSHIPPED FIRST, BEFORE ANY GOD.` · then, large: `GANESHA FIRST, BEFORE EVERY BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're about to begin: today's work, a hard conversation, a trip. Before you start it, pause. Many Hindus say a short line to Ganesha here, like Om Gam Ganapataye Namah, or simply Shri Ganesh. If you pray, say it quietly three times. If you don't, name the beginning out loud and ask for a clear path.

25.title: The race around the world
25.hook: Ganesha vs Kartikeya: one circles the earth, one circles his parents; why Hindus honor parents like gods
25.carry: circle your parents like a temple
25.tomorrow: so why is one of Ganesha's tusks snapped short?
25.howItsDone: Hindus walk pradakshina, a clockwise circle keeping the holy on their right, around temple shrines, sacred trees and the wedding fire. Many children greet parents and elders by bowing and touching their feet, and receive a blessing; this story is often told to explain why parents are honored.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesha: a new face, and Shiva's promise. Ganesha first, before every beginning. Today he gets a brother, and a race.
screen: `GANESHA FIRST, BEFORE EVERY BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: Your phone counts every step you take. It has no idea which ones mattered. Here's a race about that. Two brothers: Kartikeya, the warrior, fast and bright on his peacock, and Ganesha, round and patient on his mouse. Their parents, Shiva and Parvati, set a contest: whoever goes around the whole world first, wins. Kartikeya is gone before the sentence ends, over mountains, over oceans. Ganesha looks at his mouse. The mouse looks at Ganesha. Then Ganesha walks to his mother and father and, slowly, walks one circle around them. He bows. I'm done, he says.
screen: `YOUR PHONE COUNTS STEPS.` → `A PEACOCK AND A MOUSE.` → `HE CIRCLES HIS PARENTS.`

segments.voice: Kartikeya lands, out of breath, to find his brother already declared the winner. In the Shiva Purana, Ganesha explains: the scriptures say that walking around your parents with devotion is the same as walking around the earth. That walk has a name, pradakshina: circling something holy, keeping it on your right. Hindus do it around temple shrines, sacred trees, and the fire at a wedding. It's the body saying: this is the center, and I move around it. And Ganesha does it around his mother and father. That's the teaching: in Hinduism, parents are honored almost like gods. An old line children learn says it plainly: matru devo bhava, pitru devo bhava. Let your mother be God to you; let your father be God to you. It's why many Hindu kids bow and touch their parents' and grandparents' feet, and get a blessing back. The tellings differ on the prize: in the Shiva Purana it's who marries first; in South India it's a fruit of wisdom, and Kartikeya, called Murugan there, leaves for the hill of Palani, where pilgrims still climb to his temple. And Kartikeya isn't the fool. He really went around the world. Ganesha just knew where his world was.
screen: `MY WORLD IS RIGHT HERE.` · `PRADAKSHINA: CIRCLING THE HOLY.` · `MATRU DEVO BHAVA: YOUR MOTHER AS GOD.` · `KARTIKEYA ISN'T THE FOOL.` · then, large: `CIRCLE YOUR PARENTS LIKE A TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: Stand up, if you can, and pick a center: a photo of your parents or grandparents, or whoever raised you, or a chair where you picture them. Walk slowly around it, keeping it on your right, one step for each breath. With each circle, name one thing they gave you. Then stop and bow, the way many Hindus do at a shrine or at an elder's feet. If standing isn't possible, trace a slow circle with one finger around their names. If those relationships are hard, choose an elder who has been a blessing to you.
Pradakshina: the circle walked around something holy, keeping it on your right. One brother circled the earth. The other circled his parents.
screen: `PRADAKSHINA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Something to keep from the race: circle your parents like a temple. Ganesha's whole world was a few steps away. Until tomorrow.

26.title: The broken tusk
26.hook: Ganesha snaps his tusk to keep writing the Mahabharata; why learning is sacred and writers begin with him
26.carry: learning is sacred; ganesha gave a tusk
26.tomorrow: a god this big gets around on what, exactly?
26.howItsDone: Ganesha is honored as the lord of wisdom and learning. Many Hindus write Shri Ganesh or a line honoring him at the top of a new notebook or account book, and at Vidyarambham in Kerala a child's first written letters often begin with a prayer to Ganapati.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, pradakshina: Ganesha circled his parents as his whole world. Circle your parents like a temple. Now look closely at his face.
screen: `CIRCLE YOUR PARENTS LIKE A TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: Look at a Ganesha statue and count the tusks. One is whole. The other is snapped short, and often he's holding the broken piece in his hand. Behind that tusk is a writer's story. The sage Vyasa has a vast poem in his head, the Mahabharata, the epic that holds Krishna's battlefield line from day twenty-one, and he needs someone to write it down as he speaks. Ganesha says yes, on one condition: once I start, you can't stop. Vyasa adds his own: you can't write a line until you understand it. They begin. Somewhere in the middle, with the poem nowhere near done, the pen breaks.
screen: `COUNT THE TUSKS.` → `A POEM TOO BIG TO HOLD.` → `DON'T STOP. UNDERSTAND.` → `THE PEN BREAKS.`

segments.voice: He can't stop; that was his own rule. So, the story goes, he snaps off his own tusk, dips it in the ink and keeps writing. That's one reason he's called Ekadanta, the one with one tusk. A fact worth knowing: this scribe scene appears in some versions of the Mahabharata, but the modern critical edition, built by comparing manuscripts, leaves it out, and some Puranas explain the tusk with a fight against the warrior-sage Parashurama. So hold it as a story, not a record. But look at what Hindus took from it. Ganesha isn't only the remover of obstacles. He's the lord of wisdom and learning, the god of the written word. In Hinduism, knowledge is holy: words that teach you how to live are worth a piece of a god. And Vyasa's rule matters too. Ganesha may not write a line he doesn't understand. Sacred learning isn't speed; it's understanding. That's why many Hindu students, writers and shopkeepers open a new notebook or account book by writing Shri Ganesh at the top. In Kerala, at a ceremony called Vidyarambham, a small child's very first written words often begin with a prayer to Ganapati. Learning starts with him.

27.title: What Ganesha rides
27.hook: Ganesha catches a giant mouse and rides it instead of killing it: desire steered, not destroyed
27.carry: ganesha rides desire; it doesn't ride him
27.tomorrow: he's always got a sweet in his hand. what is it, and why?
27.howItsDone: In temples and home shrines a god's vahana often sits facing the deity, and Ganesha's mouse sits at his feet. Many Hindus keep fasts (vrat) and small vows as a way of steering desire; some devotees of Ganesha fast on Sankashti Chaturthi each month until the moon rises.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ekadanta: a tusk given so sacred words could be written down. Learning is sacred. Now look down, at his feet.
screen: `LEARNING IS SACRED; GANESHA GAVE A TUSK.`

segments.voice: Big belly, elephant head, sitting like a king, and under him, carrying all of it, a tiny mouse. Why a mouse? One well-known telling, from the Ganesha Purana: in the court of the gods, a heavenly musician named Krauncha is careless and steps on a sage's foot. The sage curses him: become a mouse. But he becomes a mouse the size of a mountain, and he tears through another sage's forest home, eating everything in sight. Ganesha throws his noose, catches the mouse and pulls it close. The mouse gives up. And Ganesha doesn't kill it. He climbs on.
screen: `A BIG GOD, A TINY MOUSE.` → `A CURSE: BECOME A MOUSE.` → `A MOUSE THE SIZE OF A MOUNTAIN.` → `CAUGHT. SPARED. RIDDEN.`

segments.voice: In this tradition, gods have animals that carry them. Shiva rides Nandi, the bull. Vishnu rides Garuda, the great eagle. Durga rides a lion. Kartikeya, from the race, has his peacock. The word is vahana, from the Sanskrit root vah, to carry, and a vahana says something about its god. So what does the mouse say? A reading many teachers give: the mouse is desire. Restless, nibbling, never full, like Krauncha eating his way through the forest. Ganesha doesn't kill it, starve it or chase it out. He catches it, sits on it and steers it. That's a real thread in Hindu teaching: the senses and their wanting aren't evil, but they make a poor master. You ride them; they don't ride you. Hindus practice this in small ways: a fast on a holy day, a vow to give something up for a season, food offered to God before it's eaten. The wanting stays. It just stops being in charge. Other Puranas tell the mouse's beginnings differently, and none is the one official story. What they share is the picture: the wise god on top, the wanting underneath, carrying him where he chooses.
screen: `VAHANA: THE ONE THAT CARRIES.` · `THE MOUNT SAYS WHO THE GOD IS.` · `NOT KILLED. STEERED.` · `A FAST, A VOW, AN OFFERING.` · then, large: `GANESHA RIDES DESIRE; IT DOESN'T RIDE HIM.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, sit still and watch for the mouse. Sooner or later a want will run through: your phone, a snack, the next thing to do. Don't chase it out, and don't obey it. Just notice it, call it wanting, and let it sit under you while you stay put. If you pray, you can offer that want to Ganesha. Some Hindus do this for a whole day with a fast; two minutes is a fine start.
Vahana: the one that carries, the animal each god rides. From vah, to carry. Ganesha's is the smallest of them all, a mouse.
screen: `VAHANA — today's word`.

28.hook: why he's always eating; the sweet as a gift that returns
28.carry: prasad: the offering comes back as grace
28.tomorrow: who would try to eat the sun for breakfast?
28.howItsDone: At temples and home shrines Hindus offer food to the deity and then share it as prasad; at Ganesh Chaturthi many families make modaks, offer them to Ganesha, and give them out to family and neighbors.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, vahana: a mouse of restless wanting, ridden and steered. Ganesha rides desire; it doesn't ride him. Today closes Ganesha's week, with the sweet in his hand.
screen: `GANESHA RIDES DESIRE; IT DOESN'T RIDE HIM.`

segments.voice: Leave a wedding or a festival and sometimes someone presses a little box into your hands: something sweet for the road. Ganesha has his own, and he never seems to put it down. In many images there's a sweet in his hand, a modak: a little dumpling of rice flour, pinched shut at the top like a flower bud, filled with coconut and jaggery. One of his names means the one who loves modaks, and at his festival, Ganesh Chaturthi, families make them by the trayful. People tell a story about that appetite. Kubera, a rich god proud of his wealth, throws Ganesha a feast to show off. Ganesha eats every dish, every pot, and he's still hungry.
screen: `A LITTLE BOX FOR THE ROAD.` → `A DUMPLING LIKE A FLOWER BUD.` → `A FEAST THAT CAN'T FILL HIM.`

segments.voice: What finally fills him is tiny: a handful of plain food, given with love. The story isn't in one fixed text; it's the kind families pass down. But it points at the word prasad: grace, a gift given freely. At a temple or a home shrine, food is offered to the god, sits before the image a while, then comes back and is shared with everyone there. Not leftovers. The same food, returned as a blessing. People often take it with the right hand, or with both hands cupped. And a detail worth repeating: in older Sanskrit, prasada also means clarity, a calm and settled mind. The gift and the grace are one word. Now hold the week up to the light. A god welcomed into clay. A mother's grief that stopped the universe. A new face, honored first. A slow circle around his parents. A broken tusk for sacred words. A mouse of wanting, steered. And a sweet, handed back as grace. Seven days with one god.
screen: `A HANDFUL, GIVEN WITH LOVE.` · `PRASAD: GRACE, GIVEN FREELY.` · `OFFERED, THEN HANDED BACK.` · `A WEEK WITH GANESHA.` · then, large: `PRASAD: THE OFFERING COMES BACK AS GRACE.`

segments.voice: If there's anything to eat near you, a piece of fruit, a cracker, a square of chocolate, hold it and smell it before anything else. Break it in two, and set half aside for someone before you taste yours. Eat your half slowly, and notice what it's like to taste something you've already given away. Some people first offer a meal to God; others offer it to the person across the table.
Prasad: grace. Food offered, then handed back as a blessing, made to be shared. The last word of the week.
screen: `PRASAD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Last line of Ganesha's week: prasad, the offering comes back as grace. Seven days, seven stories, one god.
